questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Paediatric neurology: seizures, cerebral palsy, meningitis
questions.stem: A simple febrile seizure is characterised by:
options: A generalised seizure under 15 minutes, not recurring within 24 hours, in a child aged 6 months to 5 years
Recurrence three times in one day
questions.concept: Simple febrile seizures are brief, generalised, single episodes in a neurologically normal child of 6 months to 5 years with fever. They carry an excellent prognosis and need no anticonvulsant, only parental reassurance and fever advice.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Paediatric neurology: seizures, cerebral palsy, meningitis
questions.stem: The commonest type of cerebral palsy is:
questions.concept: Spastic cerebral palsy accounts for about 70 to 80%, with spastic diplegia classically following periventricular leukomalacia in preterm infants. Dyskinetic forms follow basal ganglia injury as in kernicterus or severe asphyxia.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Paediatric neurology: seizures, cerebral palsy, meningitis
questions.stem: Cerebral palsy is best described as:
options: A non-progressive disorder of movement and posture from a static insult to the developing brain
questions.concept: The brain lesion is static and non-progressive, though the clinical picture evolves as the child grows, with contractures and deformity developing. Associated epilepsy, intellectual disability, visual, hearing and feeding problems are common.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Paediatric neurology: seizures, cerebral palsy, meningitis
questions.stem: The commonest organism causing bacterial meningitis in children beyond the neonatal period in India is:
questions.concept: Pneumococcus is the leading cause beyond the neonatal period, with Haemophilus influenzae type b and meningococcus reduced by vaccination. Group B Streptococcus, E. coli and Listeria dominate in neonates.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Paediatric neurology: seizures, cerebral palsy, meningitis
questions.stem: Cerebrospinal fluid in tuberculous meningitis typically shows:
options: Lymphocytic pleocytosis with high protein and low glucose
questions.concept: Tuberculous meningitis shows lymphocytosis, markedly raised protein with cobweb coagulum, low glucose and raised ADA, with basal exudates and hydrocephalus on imaging. Pyogenic meningitis instead shows neutrophils with very low glucose.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Paediatric neurology: seizures, cerebral palsy, meningitis
questions.stem: Dexamethasone in childhood bacterial meningitis is given to reduce:
options: Sensorineural hearing loss and neurological sequelae
questions.concept: Dexamethasone given before or with the first dose of antibiotic reduces hearing loss and neurological sequelae, particularly in Haemophilus influenzae meningitis, by blunting the inflammatory response to bacterial lysis.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Paediatric neurology: seizures, cerebral palsy, meningitis
questions.stem: Infantile spasms (West syndrome) are characterised by:
options: Clusters of flexor spasms with hypsarrhythmia on EEG and developmental regression
questions.concept: West syndrome comprises the triad of infantile spasms in clusters, hypsarrhythmia on EEG and developmental arrest or regression, usually beginning at 3 to 8 months. Treatment is ACTH, vigabatrin or corticosteroids.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Paediatric neurology: seizures, cerebral palsy, meningitis
questions.stem: Absence seizures show which characteristic EEG pattern?
questions.concept: Childhood absence epilepsy shows generalised 3 per second spike-and-wave discharges provoked by hyperventilation, with brief blank spells and no post-ictal confusion. Ethosuximide or valproate are effective; carbamazepine worsens it.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Paediatric neurology: seizures, cerebral palsy, meningitis
questions.stem: The commonest cause of acute flaccid paralysis in children now that polio is eliminated in India is:
questions.concept: With wild poliovirus eliminated, Guillain-Barre syndrome is the commonest cause of acute flaccid paralysis. Surveillance requires two stool samples from every case under 15 years to exclude poliovirus.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Paediatric neurology: seizures, cerebral palsy, meningitis
questions.stem: Neurocysticercosis in an Indian child most commonly presents with:
options: Focal seizures with a solitary ring-enhancing lesion on CT
questions.concept: Neurocysticercosis is the commonest cause of focal seizures in Indian children, typically a single small enhancing lesion with perilesional oedema. Treatment is albendazole with corticosteroids and antiepileptics.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Paediatric GIT, liver disease & malabsorption
questions.stem: Non-bilious projectile vomiting at 3 to 6 weeks of age with a palpable olive-shaped epigastric mass suggests:
questions.concept: Pyloric stenosis presents at 3 to 6 weeks with non-bilious projectile vomiting, visible gastric peristalsis and a palpable pyloric mass, causing hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. Treatment is rehydration then Ramstedt pyloromyotomy.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Paediatric GIT, liver disease & malabsorption
questions.stem: Bilious vomiting with a double-bubble sign on abdominal radiograph in a neonate indicates:
questions.concept: Duodenal atresia gives a double bubble from a dilated stomach and proximal duodenum with no distal gas, and is strongly associated with Down syndrome and polyhydramnios. Vomiting is bilious because the obstruction is distal to the ampulla.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Paediatric GIT, liver disease & malabsorption
questions.stem: A 9-month-old with paroxysmal colicky pain, redcurrant jelly stools and a sausage-shaped mass has:
questions.concept: Ileocolic intussusception peaks at 6 to 12 months, often after a viral illness with lymphoid hyperplasia. Ultrasound shows a target or doughnut sign, and pneumatic or hydrostatic reduction is both diagnostic and therapeutic if there is no peritonitis.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Paediatric GIT, liver disease & malabsorption
questions.stem: Delayed passage of meconium beyond 48 hours with abdominal distension and a tight empty rectum on examination suggests:
questions.concept: Aganglionosis of the distal bowel causes functional obstruction with delayed meconium, distension and explosive stool on withdrawal of the examining finger. Rectal biopsy showing absent ganglion cells is diagnostic.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Paediatric GIT, liver disease & malabsorption
questions.stem: The commonest cause of neonatal cholestasis requiring urgent diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Biliary atresia causes conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with pale stools and dark urine, and outcomes of the Kasai portoenterostomy fall sharply after 60 days of life, so any infant jaundiced beyond two weeks needs fractionated bilirubin urgently.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Paediatric GIT, liver disease & malabsorption
questions.stem: Necrotising enterocolitis is most common in:
options: Preterm formula-fed neonates, presenting with distension, bloody stools and pneumatosis intestinalis
questions.concept: Prematurity, enteral formula feeding and mucosal ischaemia predispose to necrotising enterocolitis, with pneumatosis intestinalis on radiograph. Feeds are stopped with nasogastric decompression and antibiotics; perforation requires surgery. Breast milk is protective.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Paediatric GIT, liver disease & malabsorption
questions.stem: Painless massive lower gastrointestinal bleeding in a toddler is most likely due to:
options: Meckel diverticulum with ectopic gastric mucosa
questions.concept: Meckel diverticulum follows the rule of 2s - 2% of population, 2 feet from the ileocaecal valve, 2 inches long, presenting before 2 years - and ectopic gastric mucosa ulcerates adjacent ileum causing painless bleeding. Technetium pertechnetate scan is diagnostic.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Paediatric GIT, liver disease & malabsorption
questions.stem: Chronic diarrhoea with steatorrhoea, recurrent chest infections and salty sweat in a child suggests:
questions.concept: CFTR dysfunction causes pancreatic exocrine insufficiency with steatorrhoea and failure to thrive, thick airway secretions with recurrent infection and raised sweat chloride. Meconium ileus at birth may be the first sign.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Paediatric GIT, liver disease & malabsorption
questions.stem: Reye syndrome, with encephalopathy and fatty liver, is associated with the use of which drug during a viral illness?
questions.concept: Aspirin during varicella or influenza is linked to Reye syndrome with mitochondrial dysfunction, vomiting, encephalopathy, raised transaminases and hyperammonaemia without jaundice, which is why aspirin is avoided under 16 years except in Kawasaki disease.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Paediatric GIT, liver disease & malabsorption
questions.stem: Wilson disease should be suspected in a child with:
options: Chronic liver disease with neuropsychiatric features and low serum ceruloplasmin
questions.concept: Wilson disease presents in older children as hepatitis, cirrhosis or fulminant failure with Coombs-negative haemolysis, and later with tremor, dystonia and behavioural change, with Kayser-Fleischer rings and raised urinary copper.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Anatomy & physiology of the ear; audiological tests
questions.stem: In Rinne's test, a negative result (bone conduction better than air conduction) indicates:
options: Conductive hearing loss in the tested ear
questions.concept: A negative Rinne means bone conduction exceeds air conduction, indicating conductive loss of at least 15 to 20 dB in that ear. In sensorineural loss, Rinne stays positive because both conductions fall together.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Anatomy & physiology of the ear; audiological tests
questions.stem: In Weber's test, lateralisation of the sound to the affected ear suggests:
options: Conductive hearing loss in that ear
questions.concept: Sound lateralises to the ear with conductive loss because masking ambient noise is reduced and bone conduction is enhanced, whereas in sensorineural loss it lateralises to the better hearing ear.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Anatomy & physiology of the ear; audiological tests
questions.stem: A type B tympanogram with a flat trace indicates:
options: Middle ear fluid as in otitis media with effusion
Eustachian tube dysfunction with negative pressure
questions.concept: A flat type B curve reflects poor compliance from middle ear fluid or a thickened drum. Type C shows negative middle ear pressure from eustachian dysfunction, and type Ad high compliance as in ossicular discontinuity.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Anatomy & physiology of the ear; audiological tests
questions.stem: The test of choice for newborn hearing screening is:
options: Otoacoustic emissions with automated brainstem response as confirmation
questions.concept: Otoacoustic emissions test outer hair cell function and require no cooperation, making them ideal for newborn screening; automated auditory brainstem response confirms and detects auditory neuropathy which OAE misses.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Anatomy & physiology of the ear; audiological tests
questions.stem: The organ of Corti is situated on the:
questions.concept: The organ of Corti rests on the basilar membrane within the scala media, with hair cells whose stereocilia contact the tectorial membrane. High frequencies are detected at the base and low frequencies at the apex - tonotopic organisation.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology, Hearing

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Anatomy & physiology of the ear; audiological tests
questions.stem: The ossicular chain amplifies sound principally by:
options: The areal ratio of tympanic membrane to stapes footplate and the lever action of the ossicles
Resonance of the external canal alone
Fluid movement in the semicircular canals
questions.concept: Impedance matching between air and cochlear fluid is achieved by a 17 to 1 areal ratio and a 1.3 to 1 ossicular lever, giving about 22 to 25 dB of gain. Loss of this mechanism produces conductive deafness.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology, Hearing

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Anatomy & physiology of the ear; audiological tests
questions.stem: Pure tone audiometry showing an air-bone gap indicates:
questions.concept: The air-bone gap quantifies the conductive component; a mixed loss shows both a raised bone conduction threshold and an air-bone gap. Speech audiometry and brainstem responses assess retrocochlear lesions.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Anatomy & physiology of the ear; audiological tests
questions.stem: Carhart's notch, a dip in bone conduction at 2000 Hz, is characteristic of:
questions.concept: Carhart's notch is an artefactual depression of bone conduction thresholds around 2 kHz caused by loss of the ossicular resonance contribution in stapes fixation, and it resolves after successful stapedectomy.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Anatomy & physiology of the ear; audiological tests
questions.stem: A 4000 Hz dip on audiometry is characteristic of:
questions.concept: Industrial noise exposure characteristically notches hearing at 4 kHz before spreading to adjacent frequencies, and is preventable by hearing protection and engineering controls; it is a compensable occupational disease.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Anatomy & physiology of the ear; audiological tests
questions.stem: Sensorineural hearing loss of ageing, affecting high frequencies bilaterally, is termed:
questions.concept: Presbycusis is bilateral symmetrical high-frequency sensorineural loss with disproportionate difficulty understanding speech in noise, managed with hearing aids and auditory rehabilitation.
